selectedConcepts.concept: Study how language works and how it shapes public life. Begin with everyday Dutch, rhetoric and the study of language and thought. Apply those perspectives to literary texts, media and social debates, with modern European history and EU politics as regional anchors.

selectedConcepts.labelRationale: Dutch, stylistics, psycholinguistics and rhetoric lead the route. Modern History and European Union Politics provide European context alongside wider cultural and social comparisons.

selectedConcepts.concept: Follow stories and images across literature, film and visual art. Move from close reading and Renaissance art to adaptation, documentary and the history of art interpretation. Use these methods to examine how identity and power are represented across societies.

selectedConcepts.labelRationale: The route progresses from literary and visual interpretation to research on narratives, film and art. The Italian Renaissance and European documentary traditions add regional examples within a wider cultural comparison.
selectedConcepts.distinctnessRationale: The literature and media and the language and society options differ by 52.5 EC each way. Literary history and criticism, myth, visual art and adaptation take the place of Dutch, psycholinguistics, EU politics and several social science courses.

selectedConcepts.concept: Study modern Europe through history, political institutions and conflict. Build from political philosophy and comparative politics to EU decision-making, international relations and research on social change. Use media and literature to explore how public debates take shape.
basisLabels: European cultures, identities, literature, text, media and comparative cultural analysis

selectedConcepts.labelRationale: Modern history, European Union Politics and comparative politics anchor the route. Historical and qualitative inquiry, peace studies and social theory support the study of political and social change.
selectedConcepts.distinctnessRationale: The politics option differs by 75 EC from the language option and 75 EC from the literature option in each direction. Its distinctive core is political philosophy, comparative politics, international relations, historical research and conflict.

audience.programmeDescription: Groningen’s degree combines study of a major European language with questions about language, literature and politics. The example shown follows German and the European Language and Society profile.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options focus on language and society, literature and media, or modern European politics. The Groningen example includes advanced language study in German.

notes.text: Groningen combines a three-course German proficiency sequence with academic study in German. The UCR options offer introductory Dutch, linguistics, literature, media or European politics in different combinations.
The UCR course options do not include a German proficiency sequence or the specialist modules taught in German. Groningen’s minor and required thesis are shown separately in the curriculum.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

ENSSUST113.name: Calling Bullshit
ENSSUST113.text: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.text: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.

GOSHIST312.text: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.text: Introduction to Political Philosophy examines political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students study views of human nature, society, rights and authority in historical context and compare their arguments with current political problems. Original texts, an essay and a group project develop interpretation and normative argument.

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.text: Provides analytical tools to compare political systems and democracies. Examines phenomena like democratic backsliding, decline of political parties, rise of populism, media changes, non‑majoritarian institutions and globalization’s impact on domestic politics.

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.text: Theory of International Relations introduces competing approaches to international relations and geopolitics, including realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism and critical theory. Students apply theories to historical and contemporary cases. A United Nations Security Council simulation develops country-position research, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.text: European Union Politics examines EU institutions, actors, integration and policymaking, including representation, legitimacy and decision-making. An empirical project investigates European Parliament committee amendments, relating MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students plan the research, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

GOSPOLI313.text: Peace & Conflict examines conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies connect to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. An interdisciplinary podcast, policy brief and research dossier develop analysis, while reflection examines how assumptions shape inquiry.

HCBCOGN312.name: Psycholinguistics
HCBCOGN312.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

MCCCOMM112.name: Dutch
MCCCOMM112.text: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.text: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.text: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
